messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Your previous vignette is missing some reported symptoms or demographic details. Rewrite it to include everything.

Previous vignette:
Dr. Robert Miller had always been a steady presence—a calm, competent emergency physician who thrived under pressure. That steadiness was shattered on a Tuesday morning two years ago, during his commute into the city. The bus he rode every day was stopped by three armed men who boarded shouting orders. Robert was ordered to the floor, then commanded to tend to a wounded accomplice who had been shot during the initial takeover. He recalls the violence—the spray of blood, the screams, the rapid-fire instructions barked at him while he worked, hands shaking, trying to keep his own breathing even. For two hours he followed orders, treating one of the attackers as the others threatened passengers at gunpoint. When police finally breached the bus, Robert was released, physically unharmed, but something inside him had been dismantled.

In the weeks that followed, he could not stop scanning the rooms of his own home. Every creak of the floorboards, every rattle of the window frame made him freeze mid-step, certain someone had entered. He began lying awake at night listening—not to his wife's breathing beside him, but to the faintest sounds beyond the bedroom door. He became convinced that the world was no longer safe, that any ordinary place—a grocery store, a waiting room, a quiet street—could suddenly turn hostile. What frightened him most was the realization that people were not what they seemed. The men on the bus had looked like anyone else before they pulled out their weapons. Now, when he passed strangers on the sidewalk, he studied their faces for signs of malice, for the subtle tension that might precede an explosion.

The trigger that was hardest to avoid was public transport. He had always taken the bus to the hospital parking lot, but after the attack he could not bring himself to stand at a bus stop. The sight of a bus pulling to the curb sent his heart racing, his palms sweating. He started driving to work every day, an extra forty minutes each way through traffic that left him irritable before he even entered the hospital. Authority commands also became a minefield. When the chief of emergency gave him orders during a busy shift—"Start the fluids, page the attending, get the chart now"—Robert felt a flash of intense anger, a surge of defiance that he barely contained. More than once he snapped at nurses or residents for what he saw as unnecessary directives. His colleagues began to keep their distance, trading glances when he walked past.

At home, his wife Patricia bore the brunt of his irritability. If she asked him a simple question while he was reading, he would bark a response, then apologize rigidly. He felt constantly on guard, even in his own living room, as though an intruder might spring from behind the sofa. He had come to believe that his life had been destroyed—not by any physical injury, but by the loss of the easy confidence he had once had. Medicine had been his calling; now he dreaded going to work, resenting the very environment that had once given him purpose. He avoided the hospital cafeteria where he had once eaten, because it was too exposed. He took the stairs instead of the elevator, because enclosed spaces made him feel trapped.

What finally brought Robert to seek help was a morning when he found himself screaming at a medical student for placing a stethoscope on the wrong spot, his voice echoing down the hall. Patricia had handed him a pamphlet for a trauma clinic and told him quietly that she couldn't keep living like this. Sitting in the waiting room now, Robert is terrified that his career is slipping away, that his marriage might not survive his anger, and that he will never feel safe again. But beneath that fear, in a part of himself he had thought dormant, there is also a thin hope—the hope that someone might help him understand why he cannot stop listening, why he cannot trust anyone, and whether the man he used to be can ever be rebuilt.

Missing items that MUST appear in the rewrite:
MISSING FROM VIGNETTE:
- Age context: The vignette does not provide any approximate age context for the patient, such as mentioning his age or age-related life stage.
- Trigger: Violence: The patient reports violence as a trigger, but the vignette does not describe any current symptom triggered by violence; it only mentions the violence during the trauma.

---

Rewrite the full vignette (4–5 paragraphs, third person) incorporating all missing items as lived clinical experience.
Preserve all content from the previous vignette that was already correct — only add what is missing.
Do not use section headers or bullet points.
